title: Web Scraping Basics (BeautifulSoup)

items.prompt: How do you parse an HTML document string using `BeautifulSoup`?
items.explanation: Instantiating `BeautifulSoup(html_doc, 'html.parser')` takes the raw HTML string and parses it into a navigable DOM tree using Python's built-in `html.parser`.

metadata.learning_objective: Initialize a BeautifulSoup DOM tree with the standard parser
metadata.common_misconception: Assuming BeautifulSoup has a separate parse_string method
metadata.why_this_exercise_exists: Essential starting point for web scraping

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly creates a BeautifulSoup object from an HTML string using the built-in parser?
items.explanation: The first argument to BeautifulSoup must be the HTML source, and the second argument must be the name of the parser to use. 'html.parser' is the correct string for Python's built-in parser. Omitting the parser name works in some cases but is not the explicit, recommended syntax shown in this lesson.

', which sequence of BeautifulSoup calls correctly extracts the price text 'Price: $10'?
items.explanation: To locate the paragraph with class 'note', you must pass class_='note' as a keyword argument to find. The .text attribute, not .get('text'), returns the inner text of the tag. Therefore, soup.find('p', class_='note').text is the correct expression.

items.prompt: Match the BeautifulSoup method to its purpose: retrieving all anchor tags, extracting visible text, and getting an attribute value.
items.explanation: find_all retrieves every matching tag, .text returns visible text, and .get retrieves an attribute value such as 'href'. These three correspond in order to the three purposes described in the prompt.

items.prompt: Which of the following is a common pitfall when scraping with BeautifulSoup?
options: Using .text when you actually need the raw HTML markup
Forgetting to install requests before importing BeautifulSoup
Using single quotes instead of double quotes in Python strings
Calling .find_all() on a string instead of a soup object
items.correct_answer: Using .text when you actually need the raw HTML markup
items.explanation: A frequent mistake is assuming .text gives you everything. If you need nested tags, comments, or raw markup, .text strips them away. You should use .prettify() or access the tag directly when raw structure matters. The other options describe either unrelated issues or not typical pitfalls for BeautifulSoup itself.

items.prompt: What is the difference in return types between `soup.find('a')` and `soup.find_all('a')`?
options: find() returns the first Tag (or None); find_all() returns a list of Tags (or empty list []).
find() returns text; find_all() returns tags.
find() returns a list; find_all() returns a generator.
There is no difference; they are aliases.
items.correct_answer: find() returns the first Tag (or None); find_all() returns a list of Tags (or empty list []).
items.explanation: `soup.find()` stops scanning after finding the first matching element and returns a single `Tag` object (or `None`). `soup.find_all()` finds every matching element in the DOM and returns a ResultSet (list) of matching tags.

metadata.learning_objective: Discriminate between single-element search (find) and multi-element search (find_all)
metadata.common_misconception: Attempting to iterate directly over the result of soup.find()
metadata.why_this_exercise_exists: Prevents TypeErrors when handling search results

items.prompt:
Why does this scraper code crash with `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'text'`? ```python soup = BeautifulSoup("

Hello

", "html.parser") heading = soup.find("h1").text ```
options: soup.find('h1') returned None because there is no <h1> in the HTML; accessing .text on None raises AttributeError.
BeautifulSoup requires lxml parser for headers.
items.correct_answer: soup.find('h1') returned None because there is no <h1> in the HTML; accessing .text on None raises AttributeError.
items.explanation: Web scraping is inherently fragile. Websites frequently change layout or omit optional elements. If a selector doesn't match, `find()` returns `None`. Safe scrapers must always verify `if elem:` before accessing `.text` or attributes.

metadata.learning_objective: Guard against AttributeError by checking if element is found
metadata.common_misconception: Assuming target elements are guaranteed to exist on every page
metadata.why_this_exercise_exists: Addresses the #1 crash in web scraper scripts

items.prompt: When searching for an element by HTML class with `soup.find()`, why must you use `class_="btn"` instead of `class="btn"`?
options: 'class' is a reserved keyword in Python, so BeautifulSoup uses 'class_' to avoid a SyntaxError.
HTML classes are underscored in Python.
There is no difference; either can be used.
items.correct_answer: 'class' is a reserved keyword in Python, so BeautifulSoup uses 'class_' to avoid a SyntaxError.
items.explanation: Because `class` is Python's reserved keyword for declaring classes, Python's parser will raise a `SyntaxError` if you try to pass `class="..."` as a keyword argument. BeautifulSoup uses `class_` with a trailing underscore as the parameter name.

metadata.why_this_exercise_exists: Eliminates a constant source of syntax errors in web scraping

items.prompt: The code below attempts to extract the first paragraph from a webpage, but it raises an error when the paragraph tag is missing. Fix the code so it safely returns an empty string instead of crashing.
items.starter_code:
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

def get_first_paragraph(url):
    r = requests.get(url)
    soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, 'html.parser')
    p = soup.find('p')
    return p.text

print(get_first_paragraph('https://example.com/missing'))
items.solution_code:
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

def get_first_paragraph(url):
    r = requests.get(url)
    soup = BeautifulSoup(r.text, 'html.parser')
    p = soup.find('p')
    if p is None:
        return ''
    return p.text

print(get_first_paragraph('https://example.com/missing'))
items.hint: Check whether `p` is `None` before calling `.text` on it.
items.explanation:
The original code assumes a `

` tag always exists. By adding `if p is None: return ''`, we prevent the `AttributeError` and make the function robust against missing content.

items.prompt: A scraper is designed to collect all links from a page, but it fails when some `<a>` tags lack an `href` attribute. Correct the code so it skips invalid links and returns only valid URLs.
items.starter_code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = '
HomeBrokenAbout
' soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') links = [a['href'] for a in soup.find_all('a')] print(links)
items.solution_code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = '
HomeBrokenAbout
' soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') links = [a['href'] for a in soup.find_all('a') if a.has_attr('href')] print(links)
items.hint: Use `has_attr('href')` to filter out `<a>` tags that do not contain an `href`.
items.explanation: List comprehensions with `a['href']` throw a `KeyError` when `href` is missing. The `if a.has_attr('href')` guard ensures only tags with the attribute are processed.

items.prompt: The function below is supposed to return a list of product names, but it incorrectly returns the entire text of each `<div>`, including nested tags. Rewrite the logic so it extracts only the clean text of each product name.
items.starter_code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = '
Product A
Product B
' soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') products = [div.text for div in soup.find_all('div')] print(products)
items.solution_code:
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup html = '
Product A
Product B
' soup = BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') products = [div.get_text(strip=True) for div in soup.find_all('div')] print(products)

items.prompt: Refactor the following scraper to improve readability, reduce redundant parsing, and add caching so repeated requests to the same URL do not hit the network again. Return a dictionary mapping each URL to its extracted titles.
items.starter_code:
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

def scrape(urls):
    results = {}
    for u in urls:
        r = requests.get(u)
        s = BeautifulSoup(r.text, 'html.parser')
        t = s.title.string
        results[u] = t
    return results

urls = ['https://a.com', 'https://b.com']
print(scrape(urls))
items.solution_code:
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

_cache = {}

def scrape(urls):
    results = {}
    for u in urls:
        if u in _cache:
            results[u] = _cache[u]
            continue
        r = requests.get(u, timeout=10)
        s = BeautifulSoup(r.text, 'html.parser')
        t = s.title.string
        _cache[u] = t
        results[u] = t
    return results

urls = ['https://a.com', 'https://b.com']
print(scrape(urls))

items.hint: Store parsed results in a module-level dictionary keyed by URL, and check the cache before calling `requests.get`.
items.explanation: The refactored version avoids redundant HTTP calls by caching results in `_cache`. It also adds a `timeout` for safety and separates concerns by checking the cache before network I/O, improving both performance and reliability.
